hook.ur: Kaltenborn–Evjenth approach mein joint par sustained traction ya glide diya jata hai.

goal.en: By the end, you'll know what Kaltenborn–Evjenth Mobilization is, when it's safe and useful, how to apply it step by step — and how to prove it worked. (3 checks along the way.)
goal.ur: End tak aap jaan jayenge ke Kaltenborn–Evjenth Mobilization kya hai, kab safe aur faida-mand hai, qadam ba qadam kaise apply hoti hai — aur kaise prove karein ke kaam kiya. (Raste mein 3 checks.)

text.en: The Kaltenborn-Evjenth approach explains which way a joint surface should glide so that a restricted movement can improve. You apply sustained or gentle traction and gliding in the joint's own 'treatment plane', using three stages that range from simply relieving pressure to stretching tight tissue.
text.ur: Is approach ka focus joint ki chhoti translatoric movements par hai, jaise traction aur glide. Traction mein joint surfaces ko ek doosray se door ki taraf load diya jata hai; glide mein ek joint surface doosri ke muqablay mein slide karti hai. Patient ko aaram-deh position mein rakhna aur relevant segment ko stabilize karna technique ka aham hissa hai.

simpler.en: Mobilization that uses joint shape (the convex-concave rule) to pick the glide direction, and traction grades to loosen, take up slack, or stretch.
simpler.ur: Kaltenborn–Evjenth approach mein joint par sustained traction ya glide diya jata hai.

text.en: A key only turns if you push it in the direction the lock expects. Joint surfaces are curved; if you know their shape, you know which way the bone must slide for the movement to open up.
text.ur: Chabi tabhi ghoomti hai jab aap usay us direction mein dhakelein jo taala expect karta hai. Joint surfaces bhi golai wali hoti hain; agar aap ko un ki shape maloom ho, to aap jaan lete hain ke movement kholne ke liye bone ko kis taraf slide karna hai.

text.en:
Three ideas carry this whole technique:
**1.** Convex-concave rule: when a convex surface moves on a concave one, the bone glides opposite to the direction the bone's shaft moves. When a concave surface moves on a convex one, the glide goes the same way as the shaft.
**2.** Three stages of traction: Stage I loosens (relieves pressure, no stretch), Stage II takes up the slack, Stage III stretches tissue.
**3.** Compare to the other side and feel the end-feel (the quality of the stop) to judge whether the joint is stiff, loose or normal.
text.ur: Sab se pehle samjhein ke limitation dard ki wajah se hai ya joint ki movement restricted hai. Relevant movement aur accessory glide ka assessment karein. Sirf joint tight lagne par mobilization select na karein; history, irritability, safety screening aur comparable movement ko saath rakhein. Treatment ke baad wohi movement dobara check karein.

text.en:
So when does **Kaltenborn–Evjenth Mobilization** make sense?
• A joint that moves less than the other side with a firm, capsular-type end-feel.
• When you need to decide glide direction logically, for example for shoulder elevation or knee extension.
• Pain-dominant joints (Stage I) and stiff joints (Stage III) in the same framework.
text.ur:
To **Kaltenborn–Evjenth Mobilization** kab samajh mein aati hai?
• A joint that moves less than the other side with a firm, capsular-type end-feel.
• When you need to decide glide direction logically, for example for shoulder elevation or knee extension.
• Pain-dominant joints (Stage I) and stiff joints (Stage III) in the same framework.

text.en:
And just as important — when you should NOT use it, or should stop:
• Unstable joints, acute fractures, active infection or inflammation, and suspected tumour.
• Hypermobile joints, where you stabilize instead of stretching.
• Any worsening neurological symptoms during the technique.
text.ur: Recent trauma, fracture ka shak, instability, active infection, severe unexplained pain ya neurological deterioration mein routine mobilization munasib nahi ho sakti. Osteoporosis, postoperative restrictions aur inflammatory flare mein extra ehtiyat chahiye. Agar response faida-mand na ho ya symptoms barhein, force ko barhane ke bajaye assessment aur plan par dobara ghour karein.

title.en: How to do it — 6 steps, each with its reason
title.ur: Kaise karein — 6 qadam, har ek ki wajah ke saath

steps.title: Find the joint and its shape
steps.detail: Example: the shoulder. The humeral head is convex and the socket is concave.

steps.title: Work out the glide direction
steps.detail: For shoulder elevation, the convex head must glide downward (inferior), opposite to the arm rising. For knee extension, the concave tibia glides forward on the convex femur.

steps.title: Compare sides and feel the end-feel
steps.detail: Test the same glide on both joints. Note which is stiffer, and whether it is painful.

steps.title: Stage I
steps.detail: Apply a small traction that just relieves joint pressure. Use this to calm pain and test sensitivity.

steps.title: Stage II then III
steps.detail: Take up the slack, then add a sustained stretch into the resistance if the joint is not irritable.

steps.title: Release slowly and retest
steps.detail: Let go gradually and re-check the original movement.

question.ur: Farz karein patient aap ke saamne hai. Aap SAB SE PEHLE kya karenge?

text.en: How much? Typical teaching range: a gentle Stage I traction held about 10 seconds for pain; for stiffness, a Stage III stretch held roughly 6-10 seconds and released, repeated several times. Adjust to the response.
text.ur:
Kitna? Dose ki teaching range:
Typical teaching range: a gentle Stage I traction held about 10 seconds for pain; for stiffness, a Stage III stretch held roughly 6-10 seconds and released, repeated several times. Adjust to the response.

beats.patient: Meena, 58, cannot lift her right arm above the shoulder after six weeks in a sling.
beats.assessment: Elevation is 100 degrees on the right and 160 on the left, stopping with a firm end-feel. Pain is mild and settles quickly.
beats.treatment: Using the convex-concave rule you apply an inferior glide of the humeral head with the arm supported, after a short Stage I traction to settle the joint, then a Stage III stretch.
beats.reassess: Elevation reaches 120 degrees. You follow with active lifting practice with a stick, then repeat within a few days.
beats.ur:
Ek misal se poora clinical flow dekhein:
Farz karein kisi patient ko wrist movement mein stiffness mehsoos hoti hai. Assessment ke baad therapist low-force traction ya glide ka short trial choose kar sakta hai aur phir wrist movement dobara check kar sakta hai. Yeh sirf concept samjhane ki fictional misal hai; har wrist problem ke liye yahi technique ya dose recommend nahi ki ja rahi.

text.en:
The mistakes I see most often:
• Applying the glide in the wrong direction because the rule was memorized, not understood.
• Stretching (Stage III) an irritable, painful joint.
• Forgetting to retest the movement.
text.ur: Aam ghalti hai zyada force lagana magar baseline record na karna. Har set ke baad pain, range aur function compare karein. Agar improvement na ho ya symptoms worsen hon, force barhane ke bajaye direction, dose ya overall plan reconsider karein.

text.en: The convex-concave rule is a useful teaching model, but real joints do not always glide exactly as predicted. Evidence for outcomes is similar to other mobilization: helpful short-term for selected patients, best with exercise.
text.ur: Is technique ko guaranteed correction ya har stiffness ka hal na kahein. Response patient aur condition ke mutabiq vary karta hai. English chapter ki evidence limitations ko patient education mein bhi honestly reflect karein.
